phases.title: Phase 1 · Foundations
phases.description: Build the operating model: scope, context, evidence, and safe control.

modules.title: The agent loop
modules.objective: Turn a request into a controlled explore–act–verify loop.
modules.simple: Claude Code is not just a chat box. It can read files, run tools, edit code, and observe results. Your job is to define the finish line and supervise the loop.
procedure: State the outcome and non-goals.
Let Claude inspect relevant evidence.
Review the proposed direction when risk is meaningful.
Require an observable check.
Inspect the diff and remaining risks.
modules.bad: Make the login better.
modules.good: Add per-IP rate limiting to POST /login. Preserve the response contract and existing dependencies. First map current middleware and tests; then implement and run focused plus full tests. Report changed files and residual risks.
modules.exercise: Rewrite one vague task from your backlog as an executable brief.
modules.success: Another engineer can tell exactly what success, boundaries, and verification mean.

quiz.question: What most reliably improves autonomous work?
quiz.explanation: External evidence closes the correction loop.

modules.title: Prompts that survive contact with code
modules.objective: Provide sufficient context without micromanaging implementation.
modules.simple: Specify what matters: outcome, evidence, constraints, scope, and checks. Let repository conventions fill in the rest.
procedure: Name the user-visible outcome.
Point to starting evidence or ask Claude to find it.
List invariants and non-goals.
Define verification.
Invite questions only for material ambiguity.
modules.bad: Make it cleaner and production ready.
modules.good: Refactor the CSV parser to handle quoted newlines without changing its exported API. Follow existing error conventions. Add regression tests from these two examples; run the parser test group and typecheck. Avoid new dependencies.
modules.exercise: Add two explicit non-goals and one measurable check to a prompt.
modules.success: The prompt constrains behavior but does not dictate every code line.

quiz.question: Which detail is usually least useful?
quiz.explanation: Terms like ‘better’ or ‘cleaner’ have no observable boundary.

modules.title: Map an unfamiliar repository
modules.objective: Build a trustworthy map before editing.
modules.simple: Ask for structure, entry points, data flow, conventions, and test commands—each tied to files.
procedure: Read project instructions and top-level docs.
Inspect manifests and build commands.
Trace one representative request or execution path.
Find adjacent tests and recent relevant history.
Write a map with file references and uncertainties.
modules.bad: Read every file and explain the repo.
modules.good: Map the authentication request path from entry point to persistence. Cite files and symbols, identify the test seam, and list uncertainties. Do not edit.
modules.exercise: Produce a five-file evidence map for one feature.
modules.success: You can predict which files and checks a small change would touch.

quiz.question: Why avoid reading every file?
options: It creates noisy context without a question
quiz.explanation: Repository exploration should follow a hypothesis or execution path.

phases.title: Phase 2 · Productive delivery
phases.description: Plan, implement, test, debug, and review in tight loops.

modules.title: Plans that produce reviewable slices
modules.objective: Convert a feature into ordered, independently verifiable increments.
modules.simple: A useful plan names files, decisions, checks, and rollback points—not just activities.
procedure: Explore current behavior.
Compare the simplest viable options.
Choose and record constraints.
Split by behavior and verification boundary.
Implement one slice at a time.
modules.bad: 1. Update backend 2. Update frontend 3. Test.
modules.good: Slice 1: add failing service test and minimal domain behavior. Slice 2: expose existing-style endpoint and contract test. Slice 3: connect UI state and browser check.
modules.exercise: Split a cross-stack feature into three demonstrable slices.
modules.success: Each slice can be reviewed and reverted independently.

quiz.question: The best split boundary is usually…
quiz.explanation: Behavioral slices create meaningful checkpoints.

modules.title: Evidence-first debugging
modules.objective: Move from symptom to proven root cause.
modules.simple: Reproduce first. Then reduce the search area and try to disprove competing explanations.
procedure: Capture exact symptom and environment.
Create the smallest reliable reproduction.
Trace from observed boundary inward.
List competing hypotheses and discriminating evidence.
Fix the cause, retain a regression test, run broader checks.
modules.bad: The test is flaky. Fix timing.
modules.good: Reproduce the failure 20 times, compare passing and failing logs, identify shared state, and test the leading two hypotheses before editing production code.
modules.exercise: Write two falsifiable hypotheses for a recent bug.
modules.success: The fix explains all observed evidence and the old behavior now fails a regression test.

quiz.question: What comes before a fix?
quiz.explanation: Without a reproduction, you cannot prove the fix addresses the symptom.

modules.title: Context and session control
modules.objective: Recognize context decay and recover without losing durable state.
modules.simple: Start fresh between unrelated tasks. For long work, save a compact handoff before clearing or branching.
procedure: Watch for repeated mistakes, forgotten constraints, or irrelevant history.
Stop the current action early.
Record goal, decisions, files, evidence, failures, and next step.
Compact or start a named fresh session.
Verify the new session’s understanding before edits.
modules.bad: Continue correcting the same misunderstanding indefinitely.
modules.good: Create HANDOFF.md with current state and test evidence; start fresh and ask the new session to validate the handoff against the repository.
modules.exercise: Write a context handoff in under 200 words.
modules.success: A fresh agent can name the next action and critical constraints without the old transcript.

quiz.question: When is /clear safest?
quiz.explanation: Durable state prevents context reset from becoming knowledge loss.

modules.title: Git and review as control surfaces
modules.objective: Make every agent change inspectable and reversible.
modules.simple: Use status, diff, tests, focused commits, and draft PRs as explicit gates.
procedure: Confirm the intended branch and clean baseline.
Review status before and after edits.
Inspect the complete diff, including generated files.
Run required checks.
Commit coherently and open a draft PR with evidence.
modules.bad: Commit and push everything.
modules.good: Show status and diff summary; identify unrelated changes; run the documented checks; propose a commit message; wait before push.
modules.exercise: Review a diff for scope, behavior, tests, and security separately.
modules.success: Every changed line belongs to the stated objective and has an appropriate check.

quiz.question: Why is a checkpoint not a Git replacement?
options: It may not capture Bash or external changes
quiz.explanation: Git is the durable record across all change mechanisms.

modules.title: Harness engineering: from demo to dependable system
modules.objective: Identify every system surrounding the model.
modules.simple: A prompt is one component. A dependable agent also needs controlled context, tools, state, memory, evaluation, permissions, traces, retry rules, and stopping conditions.
procedure: Draw the agent boundary and goal.
List context inputs and tools.
Choose durable state and memory.
Define evaluation and stop conditions.
Add permissions, tracing, and recovery.
modules.bad: Use a smart model and keep retrying until it works.
modules.good: Design the complete loop: explicit state, typed tools, outcome evaluator, bounded retries, logs, and a human escalation path.
modules.exercise: Draw a harness diagram for one automation you use.
modules.success: Every arrow has an owner, observable output, and failure path.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a production harness from a demo?
options: Explicit feedback, state, safety, and observability
quiz.explanation: Reliability comes from the surrounding system, not model capability alone.

modules.title: Daily Claude Code interface mastery
modules.objective: Reduce friction in frequent interactions.
modules.simple: Status and context visibility prevent accidental branch/session mistakes; voice captures detailed intent; aliases, concise output, history search, and background work reduce repeated overhead.
procedure: Learn essential slash commands and input editing.
Expose model, directory, branch, dirty state, and context usage.
Use voice for rich briefs, then review transcription.
Ask for compact file/log slices.
Name and search sessions.
Background only bounded long-running work.
Adopt one customization at a time.
modules.bad: Install every customization and patch before doing real work.
modules.good: Track recurring friction for a week, then add the smallest alias/status/voice improvement and verify it saves time without adding risk.
modules.exercise: Measure one repeated interaction and remove two unnecessary steps.
modules.success: The improvement is used repeatedly and does not broaden authority.

quiz.question: Why customize the status line?
options: To expose branch, worktree, and context state before acting
quiz.explanation: Visible state prevents coordination errors.

phases.title: Phase 3 · Advanced systems
phases.description: Build reusable context, integrations, parallelism, and bounded autonomy.

modules.title: CLAUDE.md as executable team memory
modules.objective: Maintain concise instructions that measurably change behavior.
modules.simple: Add a rule when a non-obvious instruction repeats. Remove it when stale or inferable.
procedure: Start minimal.
Add exact commands and non-obvious constraints.
Choose global, project, local, or child scope.
Commit shared instructions.
Test whether behavior changes; prune periodically.
modules.bad: Always write good, clean, secure code. Here is every file in the project…
modules.good: Run `npm test -- --runInBand` on Windows CI. Never edit `src/generated`; run `npm run generate`. API errors use `ProblemDetails` from `src/http/errors.ts`.
modules.exercise: Delete three generic lines and replace one recurring correction with a concrete rule.
modules.success: The file is short, current, scoped, and answers questions the repository cannot.

quiz.question: Where should temporary task progress live?
quiz.explanation: Project instructions are for stable guidance, not ephemeral state.

modules.title: Skills, hooks, MCP, and subagents
modules.objective: Choose the smallest extension mechanism that fits.
modules.simple: Rules are memory; skills are methods; hooks are deterministic events; MCP is an external bridge; subagents isolate cognition.
procedure: Name the missing capability.
Decide whether it is always-on, on-demand, event-driven, external, or isolated.
Choose one mechanism.
Limit scope and permissions.
Measure context and maintenance cost.
modules.bad: Install a large plugin collection because it might be useful.
modules.good: Create an on-demand `release-check` skill with a read-only script; keep deployment approval outside it.
modules.exercise: Classify five recurring tasks by extension type.
modules.success: Each extension has a clear trigger, narrow authority, and owner.

quiz.question: What best fits deterministic formatting after edits?
quiz.explanation: Hooks run deterministic actions at defined lifecycle events.

modules.title: Parallel work without collisions
modules.objective: Scale throughput while keeping ownership and integration clear.
modules.simple: Parallelize independent investigation or branches; serialize shared design and integration.
procedure: Draw task dependencies.
Assign non-overlapping read/write scopes.
Use worktrees for concurrent edits.
Require concise evidence-based outputs.
Integrate and verify centrally.
modules.bad: Send four agents to refactor the same module.
modules.good: One agent maps data migration risk; one reviews security; one implements in a worktree; the lead integrates after both reports.
modules.exercise: Mark a feature graph with parallel and serial nodes.
modules.success: No two writers own the same files and every branch has an integration check.

quiz.question: What limits parallelism most often?
quiz.explanation: Conflicting edits and decisions erase concurrency gains.

modules.title: Permission design and isolation
modules.objective: Increase useful autonomy without expanding blast radius.
modules.simple: Approve categories you understand, keep irreversible actions explicit, and isolate experiments.
procedure: Inventory tools, data, network, and credentials.
Classify actions by reversibility and impact.
Allowlist exact safe commands.
Sandbox risky long-running work.
Review logs, outputs, and approved rules.
modules.bad: Use skip-permissions on the host for convenience.
modules.good: Run the experiment in a disposable container with only the repository mounted, no production credentials, and a diff-based export path.
modules.exercise: Create a permission matrix for tests, package install, push, and deploy.
modules.success: A mistaken command cannot reach unrelated files, secrets, or production.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to increase autonomy?
quiz.explanation: Isolation limits consequences independent of intent.

modules.title: Context, state, and memory architecture
modules.objective: Store the right information in the right place.
modules.simple: Context is ephemeral working input. State tracks workflow progress. Memory preserves selected facts or patterns across runs. Mixing them creates bloated prompts and stale truth.
procedure: Classify each datum as context, state, memory, or source of truth.
Keep authoritative state outside chat.
Write memory only after validation.
Attach provenance and expiry.
Rehydrate a fresh context from minimal state.
modules.bad: Keep the full transcript forever so the agent remembers.
modules.good: Store task status in structured JSON, validated conventions in a small memory file, and load only relevant source material into each iteration.
modules.exercise: Classify ten pieces of session information into context/state/memory.
modules.success: A fresh run resumes correctly without the previous transcript.

quiz.question: Where should “task 4 passed” live?
quiz.explanation: Progress is state, not a timeless instruction.

modules.title: Tool and interface design
modules.objective: Give agents narrow, predictable hands.
modules.simple: Tools should expose one coherent capability with explicit input, structured output, useful errors, and least privilege. CLI and MCP are delivery mechanisms, not goals.
procedure: Start from the missing capability.
Prefer an established CLI or API.
Define input/output schemas.
Constrain authority and time.
Test success, failure, and adversarial inputs.
modules.bad: Give the agent a generic shell and tell it to be careful.
modules.good: Expose a read-only get_ci_failure(run_id) operation returning job, step, excerpt, and source URL; keep retry and mutation outside it.
modules.exercise: Redesign one broad tool as two narrow operations.
modules.success: Invalid calls fail clearly and the tool cannot affect unrelated resources.

quiz.question: What is the first reason to add MCP?
options: A needed external capability lacks a better narrow interface
quiz.explanation: Choose integration by capability gap and permission boundary.

modules.title: Orchestration and multi-agent systems
modules.objective: Coordinate work without multiplying confusion.
modules.simple: Orchestration is dependency management: who does what, in which order, with what handoff and integration gate. Multiple agents are useful only for separable work.
procedure: Draw task dependencies.
Keep shared decisions with one owner.
Fan out independent read/review tasks.
Isolate writers in worktrees.
Validate outputs against contracts.
Integrate centrally.
modules.bad: Launch five agents on the same feature and merge what looks best.
modules.good: One lead owns architecture; independent agents map security and tests; one isolated writer implements; the lead reconciles evidence and runs integration checks.
modules.exercise: Turn a project into a dependency graph and label parallel nodes.
modules.success: No overlapping write ownership; every handoff has a schema and acceptance check.

quiz.question: When should two agents work in parallel?
options: When their work is independent and outputs can be integrated
When they edit the same file
quiz.explanation: Independence and explicit integration are the prerequisites.

modules.title: Guardrails, permissions, and human gates
modules.objective: Place control at the point of consequence.
modules.simple: Guardrails encode prohibited behavior, permissions limit reachable actions, and human gates reserve consequential decisions. Each layer covers different failures.
procedure: Inventory assets and side effects.
Classify actions by impact and reversibility.
Constrain filesystem/network/tool scope.
Automate safe reads and checks.
Require approval before irreversible or external actions.
Log overrides.
modules.bad: Ask for approval on everything—or skip all permissions.
modules.good: Auto-run local tests in a sandbox, allow read-only issue lookup, and require approval for push, deploy, deletion, or sending messages.
modules.exercise: Create a permission matrix for your workflow.
modules.success: A mistaken instruction cannot reach secrets, unrelated files, or production.

quiz.question: Which action most clearly needs a human gate?
quiz.explanation: Deployment has external and potentially irreversible impact.

modules.title: Evals, observability, and tracing
modules.objective: Know whether the agent succeeded and why.
modules.simple: An eval scores outcomes against a dataset or rubric. Observability records the execution path—context, tool calls, state, retries, latency, cost, and overrides.
procedure: Define representative tasks and expected outcomes.
Record tool/state transitions with correlation IDs.
Track quality, cost, latency, retries, and overrides.
Separate model failure from tool/data failure.
Regression-test changes to prompts, tools, or models.
modules.bad: It worked on my last prompt, so ship it.
modules.good: Run a versioned task set, compare pass rate and cost, and inspect traces for regressions before rollout.
modules.exercise: Design five eval cases including one adversarial failure.
modules.success: A regression is reproducible and traceable to a component or step.

quiz.question: What does observability add beyond a pass/fail eval?
options: The execution evidence explaining the outcome
quiz.explanation: Traces explain how and where an outcome was produced.

modules.title: Stopping conditions, reflection, and recovery
modules.objective: Ensure every loop can finish safely.
modules.simple: Reflection is useful only when it compares evidence with a rule. A loop needs verified success, terminal failure, time/cost/attempt budgets, and escalation exits.
procedure: Define machine-checkable success.
Set maximum attempts, time, and cost.
Name terminal errors and forbidden actions.
Reflect against evidence after each iteration.
Escalate ambiguity rather than retrying it.
Preserve trace and partial state.
modules.bad: Keep trying until you are confident.
modules.good: Exit on passing acceptance checks; stop after three failed attempts or budget; escalate permissions and ambiguous requirements to a person.
modules.exercise: Write success and failure exits for one agent loop.
modules.success: Every execution ends in verified success, explicit failure, or owned escalation.

quiz.question: What is a safe stopping design?
options: Success plus budgets, terminal failures, and escalation
quiz.explanation: A phrase alone can be emitted falsely; independent checks and hard bounds are required.

modules.title: CLAUDE.md hierarchy and progressive disclosure
modules.objective: Build concise instructions that load at the correct scope.
modules.simple: A hierarchy lets global preferences, team rules, personal overrides, and subsystem guidance remain separate. The root is an index, not a warehouse.
procedure: Start with observed repeated corrections.
Choose global, root, local, or child scope.
Keep core commands and non-obvious invariants concise.
Link detailed references progressively.
Use deterministic tools for style enforcement.
Review and prune on repository changes.
modules.bad: Put 200 rules, every directory description, lint style, and current task in the root file.
modules.good: Root: commands and invariants. Child frontend file: UI-specific rules. Local file: personal setup. Hook: formatter enforcement. Handoff: current task state.
modules.exercise: Refactor a bloated instruction file into four destinations.
modules.success: Each rule loads only where relevant and measurably changes behavior.

quiz.question: Where should frontend-only exceptions live?
quiz.explanation: Narrow scope reduces noise and unintended application.

modules.title: Research, writing, browser, and DevOps workflows
modules.objective: Use the terminal as a universal interface while preserving verification.
modules.simple: Claude Code can orchestrate search, files, Markdown, CI logs, browsers, APIs, and artifacts. The common pattern is durable input, established tools, and independent evidence.
procedure: Save source material and URLs.
Choose the direct CLI/API/browser tool.
Ask for structured sourced output.
Keep writing in reviewable Markdown.
For CI, reproduce and inspect history/flakiness.
For UI, combine DOM/accessibility checks with screenshots.
Use draft PRs or artifacts as review gates.
modules.bad: Research this, fix CI, and publish the result.
modules.good: Collect cited evidence, produce a Markdown draft, diagnose CI with focused logs and history, verify changes, then create a draft PR without pushing or publishing automatically.
modules.exercise: Turn one research result into a cited Markdown note and a verified action plan.
modules.success: Claims have sources; commands/results are recorded; external publication remains reviewed.

quiz.question: What is the safest publication workflow?
options: Durable draft, evidence review, then explicit approval
quiz.explanation: A reviewable artifact separates generation from external action.

phases.title: Phase 4 · Expert operating system
phases.description: Turn reliable personal loops into team-scale, reviewable automation.

modules.title: Automate the automation
modules.objective: Encode a proven loop with machine-checkable boundaries.
modules.simple: Automate after the manual loop is reliable and its failure states are understood.
procedure: Run the workflow manually and collect failures.
Define inputs, schema, timeouts, and authority.
Use non-interactive mode for bounded analysis.
Validate outputs deterministically.
Require approval at high-impact boundaries and monitor drift.
modules.bad: Give an unattended agent repository and production access.
modules.good: CI sends a bounded diff to a read-only reviewer, validates JSON findings, and posts a report; humans approve any mutation.
modules.exercise: Add failure, timeout, and rollback behavior to an automation design.
modules.success: The automation fails closed, produces auditable evidence, and has a named owner.

quiz.question: What should be automated first?
quiz.explanation: Known loops have defined inputs, checks, and recovery.

modules.title: Independent verification systems
modules.objective: Reduce correlated mistakes between authoring and review.
modules.simple: A fresh context, different evidence, or deterministic tool can challenge assumptions the authoring session inherited.
procedure: Freeze the candidate diff.
Give the reviewer requirements and repository—not the author’s rationale first.
Ask for falsification and line-level evidence.
Run independent tests and security checks.
Reconcile findings and document residual risk.
modules.bad: Ask the same session: Is your code correct?
modules.good: In a fresh worktree session, review the diff against the issue, search for callers, run adversarial tests, and report only evidenced findings.
modules.exercise: Design a writer/reviewer/tester triangle for a risky change.
modules.success: At least two independent evidence paths support the result.

quiz.question: Why use a fresh reviewer?
quiz.explanation: Fresh context is less committed to the original assumptions.

modules.title: Your evolving Claude Code operating manual
modules.objective: Build a durable system from observed successes and failures.
modules.simple: Capture only repeatable leverage: prompts, checks, rules, skills, and failure recoveries that proved useful.
procedure: Log costly failures and repeated corrections.
Turn recurring guidance into the smallest durable artifact.
Measure acceptance, rework, test failures, and cycle time.
Review instructions and permissions monthly.
Retire tools that add context or maintenance without measurable benefit.
modules.bad: Accumulate every community tip and plugin.
modules.good: After three similar CI investigations, create a read-only triage skill with evidence fields; compare its findings for a month before automating comments.
modules.exercise: Choose one repeated correction and design its durable home.
modules.success: Your system becomes simpler while success rate and recovery speed improve.

quiz.question: What belongs in a long-term manual?
quiz.explanation: Local evidence matters more than novelty.

modules.title: Ralph loops and overnight builds
modules.objective: Use file-based iteration without unbounded autonomy.
modules.simple: Ralph repeatedly works one atomic story, tests it, records progress, and continues. Its value is fresh context plus durable state—not blind repetition.
procedure: Write and review a PRD.
Convert it to atomic stories with passes:false.
Define executable acceptance checks.
Work one story per iteration.
Update state and progress notes only after checks pass.
Stop on completion, budget, terminal error, or human gate.
Run inside an isolated environment.
modules.bad: Build my whole SaaS overnight. Say DONE when finished.
modules.good: In a disposable worktree/container, implement the next failing story only; run named checks; set passes:true only when they pass; stop after 12 iterations or $X.
modules.exercise: Design a three-story Ralph task file and hard-stop policy.
modules.success: A false DONE cannot terminate the loop, and a bad trajectory cannot run indefinitely.

quiz.question: What makes a Ralph loop trustworthy?
options: Atomic work, external checks, durable state, and hard limits
quiz.explanation: Verification and boundaries—not persistence alone—make it useful.

modules.title: Hooks, subagents, skills, and MCP together
modules.objective: Compose extension mechanisms by responsibility.
modules.simple: CLAUDE.md tells; hooks enforce deterministic events; skills package on-demand methods; subagents isolate cognition; MCP bridges external capabilities.
procedure: Name the missing behavior.
Classify it as instruction, deterministic event, reusable method, isolated work, or external capability.
Choose one mechanism first.
Limit trigger and authority.
Test failure and uninstall paths.
modules.bad: Install a plugin bundle and place all instructions in CLAUDE.md.
modules.good: Hook blocks secret access; skill describes security review; read-only subagent performs it; MCP retrieves issue context; root CLAUDE.md states when to use the workflow.
modules.exercise: Map five recurring jobs to the smallest mechanism.
modules.success: No mechanism duplicates another and each has a clear owner and permission boundary.

quiz.question: What should enforce formatting after every edit?
quiz.explanation: Formatting is deterministic event-driven work.

modules.title: Graphify, Obsidian, and provenance-linked knowledge
modules.objective: Turn document collections into a reversible, sourced second brain.
modules.simple: A knowledge graph models ideas as nodes and relationships as edges. Obsidian makes them navigable, but usefulness depends on provenance and retrieval—not note volume.
procedure: Start in an isolated vault or deletable folder.
Ingest an explicit source set.
Extract concepts and typed relationships.
Create one note per useful concept.
Backlink every note to source and location.
Enrich bare notes with sourced summaries.
Define review, retrieval, and refresh routines.
Merge into the main vault only after audit.
modules.bad: Generate 600 linked titles directly inside my main vault.
modules.good: Build an isolated vault, preserve source documents, attach provenance to every node, sample-check edges, then import one removable folder.
modules.exercise: Create a five-document mini graph with source backlinks.
modules.success: Every claim is traceable and the entire import can be removed cleanly.

quiz.question: What prevents graph-based synthesis from becoming unsupported?
options: Source provenance on nodes and claims
quiz.explanation: Backlinks allow every synthesis to be checked against origin.
